stem: Radiation of intensity \(0.5 \times 10^{-4}\) W/m\(^2\) falls on the emitter in a photoelectric set-up. The emitter (cathode) is made up of potassium and has an area of 5 cm\(^2\). Let us assume that the electrons from only the surface are knocked off by the radiation. According to the wave theory, what will be the time required to notice some deflection in the microammeter connected in the circuit? (Given the metallic radius of potassium atom is 230 pm and work function of potassium is 2.3 eV.)
solution:
Given
Intensity of radiation \(= 0.5 \times 10^{-4}\) W/m\(^2\),
Area of cathode \(= 5\) cm\(^2 = 5 \times 10^{-4}\) m\(^2\).
Radius of potassium atom \(= 230\) pm \(= 230 \times 10^{-12}\) m
Work function of potassium \(= 2.3\) eV \(= 2.3 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\) J

The number \(N\) of electrons present on the surface of cathode can be approximately calculated assuming that each potassium atom contributes one electron and the radius of potassium atom is \(230 \times 10^{-12}\) m.

\(N =\) Area of cathode / area covered by one atom
\(= 5 \times 10^{-4} / (3.1415 \times 230 \times 10^{-12} \times 230 \times 10^{-12})\)
\(= 3008 \times 10^{12}\)

Incident power on the cathode is
\(= 0.5 \times 10^{-4}\) W/m\(^2 \times 5 \times 10^{-4}\) m\(^2\)
\(= 2.5 \times 10^{-8}\) W

Wave theory assumes that this power distributed over the whole area of the cathode is uniformly absorbed by all the electrons. Therefore the energy absorbed by each electron in one second is
\(= 2.5 \times 10^{-8}\) W \(/\, 3009 \times 10^{12} \approx 8.311 \times 10^{-24}\) W.

Work function of potassium is
\(2.30\) eV \(= 2.30 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\) J \(= 3.68 \times 10^{-19}\) J.

Hence each electron will require minimum \(3.68 \times 10^{-19}\) J of energy to be knocked off from the surface of the cathode.

The time required to accumulate this energy will be
\(3.68 \times 10^{-19}\) J \(/\, 8.31 \times 10^{-24}\) W
\(= 4.428 \times 10^{4}\) s, which is about half a day.

stem:
(a) Calculate the energies of photons corresponding to ultraviolet light and red light, given that their wavelengths are 3000 \(\mathring{A}\) and 7000 \(\mathring{A}\) respectively. (Remember that the photon are not coloured. Colour is human perception for that frequency range.)
(b) A typical FM radio station has its broadcast frequency 98.3 MHz. What is the energy of an FM photon of this frequency?
solution:
Given
\(\lambda_{uv} = 3000\, \mathring{A} = 3000 \times 10^{-10}\) m,
\(\lambda_{red} = 7000\, \mathring{A} = 7000 \times 10^{-10}\) m and
\(\nu_{FM} = 98.3\) MHz \(= 98.3 \times 10^{6}\) s\(^{-1}\)

We know that energy \(E\) of electromagnetic radiation of frequency \(\nu\) is \(h\nu\) and if \(\lambda\) is the corresponding wavelength, then \(\lambda\nu = c\), \(c\) being the speed of electromagnetic radiation in vacuum.

Hence, \(E = h\nu = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda}\)

(a)
\(E = \dfrac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J s} \times 3 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1}}{3000 \times 10^{-10}\ \text{m}}\)
\(= 6.63 \times 10^{-19}\) J \(= 4.144\) eV
for a photon corresponding to ultraviolet light and

\(E = \dfrac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J s} \times 3 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1}}{7000 \times 10^{-10}\ \text{m}}\)
\(= 2.84 \times 10^{-19}\) J \(= 1.776\) eV
for a photon corresponding to red light.

(b) The energy of photon of FM frequency 98.3 MHz is \(6.63 \times 10^{-34}\) J s \(\times\ 98.3 \times 10^{6}\) s\(^{-1}\)
\(= 651.73 \times 10^{-28}\) J \(= 40.74 \times 10^{-8}\) eV.

This is very small energy as compared to the photon energy in the visible range.

stem: The wavelength and power of the incident light is 4000 \(\mathring{A}\) and 0.1 W respectively. What is the minimum change in the energy of the incident light? What is the number of incident photons?
solution:
Given incident intensity \(= 0.1\) W and \(\lambda = 4000\, \mathring{A} = 4000 \times 10^{-10}\) m.

The energy \(E\) of a photon of given wavelength is
\(E = h\nu = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \dfrac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J s} \times 3 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m/s}}{4000 \times 10^{-10}\ \text{m}}\)
\(= 4.972 \times 10^{-19}\) J

This is the minimum change in energy and is very small. The change in energy can therefore be considered as continuous.

Number of photons \(N\) incident per second is
\(N = \dfrac{0.1\ \text{W}}{4.97 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{J}} \approx 2.011 \times 10^{17}\)

The number of photons coming out is so large that human eye cannot comprehend or count it. Even if one wishes to count, say 10 photons per second, \(\sim 10^{9}\) years will be required.
